extracted.intended_audience: researchers and clinicians who act as peer reviewers for biomedical journals (novice and experienced reviewers, journal editors selecting reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers performing peer review of biomedical journal submissions, covering who should review, ethical responsibilities, how to structure reviewer comments, and practical skills to produce constructive evidence-based critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept reviewer invitations only if able to timely submit comments; monitoring and reporting average peer review timelines is required; first-round reviews may last from a few days to a few weeks; fast-track reviews (up to 3 days) exist for priority items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely reviewer accomplishments enable fast publication and avoid ethical problems (e.g., plagiarism of a manuscript under evaluation). Unjustifiably long peer review is unethical; unjustifiably short review may indicate absence of quality evaluation and predatory publishing. Journals should monitor/report timelines to encourage timely evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and ethical conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must keep confidentiality and conduct evaluations ethically, avoiding biased or unfair evaluations and other forms of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow global editorial recommendations (e.g., ICMJE, CSE, COPE, WAME). Disclose financial and non‑financial conflicts of interest (use ICMJE forms where applicable). Decline invitations if conflicts cannot be managed. Editors should employ mechanisms to disclose reviewer conflicts and process negative comments cautiously. Avoid manipulations (fake reviews) and coercive behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer qualifications and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The best reviewers are active researchers with extensive subject-matter experience and an impressive list of relevant and recent publications; ideally peers of the manuscript authors with equal scholarly ranks and credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All authors with relevant profiles may act as reviewers; editors may engage junior researchers as co-reviewers with mentors. Validated profiles (e.g., ORCID) and presence on reviewer platforms (Publons) help select and validate reviewers. Editors should prioritize selecting skilled reviewers with validated profiles to avoid substandard or fraudulent comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting standards and bibliographic resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should adhere to research reporting standards (EQUATOR Network) and have access to bibliographic databases to draft evidence-based and detailed comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate methodology and suggest revisions in line with reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT, PRISMA). Perform up-to-date literature searches to assess novelty and context. Journal editorial systems may provide links to reporting checklists and databases to support reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical competence and data presentation checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should have statistical skills to detect basic mistakes and problems in data presentation (e.g., incorrect reporting of means and standard deviations) and suggest appropriate analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scan tables and figures for presentation errors; recommend re-analyses or replacement of parametric tests with non-parametric ones when distributions warrant. Point out incomplete or inaccurate statistical analyses and request corrections or clarifications supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of a reviewer comment (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: An optimal reviewer comment should comprehensively examine all parts of the research and review work, following a structured format (see Table I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the suggested sections: Introductory line, Evaluation of title/abstract/keywords, Major comments, Minor comments, Concluding remarks. Ensure comments are evidence-based, cover methodology, ethics, novelty, and implications, and are clearly organized for authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory line
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarizes the overall impression about the manuscript validity and implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin reviews with a concise summary judgment (e.g., major strengths/weaknesses, whether manuscript is acceptable in principle). This orients authors and editors to the reviewer’s main view before detailed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of title, abstract and keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the title correctness and completeness, inclusion of all relevant keywords, presence of study design terms, appropriate information load, and relevance and adequacy of the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest title edits to reflect study scope/design and ensure keywords enable discoverability. Check that the abstract accurately reflects methods, results, and conclusions and contains essential keywords and design descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major comments (content and standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Major comments should specifically analyse each manuscript part in line with reporting standards, support suggestions with solid evidence, weigh novelty and methodological rigour, highlight the choice of study design, and point to missing/incomplete ethics approval, rights to reuse graphics, accuracy/completeness of statistical analyses, and professionalism of bibliographic searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed, evidence-backed critiques (cite guidelines or literature when suggesting methodological or analytic changes). Flag ethical or regulatory oversights (e.g., missing ethics statements, consent). Prioritize issues that affect validity and interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor comments identify language mistakes, typos, inappropriate format of graphics and references, length of texts and tables, use of supplementary material, unusual sections and order, completeness of scholarly contribution, conflict of interest, and funding statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize these as minor to avoid overemphasis on copy-editing; provide line-level or page/paragraph locators for easy revision. Recognize that language issues are usually minor given availability of editing services, but flag severe language problems that impede comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on take-home messages and implications of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize what should be done to improve the manuscript and the reviewer’s final recommendation (accept/minor revision/major revision/reject) with rationale. Keep concluding remarks succinct and tied to earlier points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope boundaries for reviewer recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should avoid engaging in the authors’ research and writing beyond providing critique; they should refrain from instructing authors on additional tests and data collection that would delay publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend clarifications or re-analyses rather than requesting entirely new experiments/data unless essential for validity. Avoid prescribing extensive new work that effectively asks authors to conduct new studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing recommendations to editors (accept/reject/transfer and ethics concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are encouraged to submit recommendations on manuscript acceptance/rejection and related editorial tasks, and to raise ethics concerns to editors, but their recommendations do not replace editors’ decision-making authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending rejection or transfer, explain grounds (e.g., out of scope, fatal methodological flaws). Alert editors to suspected ethical issues (e.g., plagiarism, undisclosed conflicts, fabricated data) and provide evidence or rationale in confidential comments to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone, clarity and professionalism of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be properly edited, conveyed in positive or neutral tones, express ideas with appropriate degrees of certainty, and present logical order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rude or aggressive language. Be constructive and collegial. Non-native English speakers should consider language guidance or consulting linguists. Organize points from major to minor and be explicit about what changes are required versus suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and awareness of peer review model
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand advantages and disadvantages of peer review models (in-house, single-blind, double-blind, open/public, post-publication review, social media commenting) and their implications for bias, transparency, and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open/public review may increase accountability; double-blind reduces identity-based bias but is burdensome; single-blind may expose reviewers to bias via author information. Reviewers and editors should choose models aligned with journal priorities and the open science movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and preventing peer-review manipulation (fake reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be vigilant about fake peer review and manipulation; practical options to prevent include assigning independent reviewers and requesting ORCID IDs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should validate reviewer identities, avoid author-suggested reviewers without independent verification, and require verified profiles. Reviewers and editors should report suspected manipulations and follow publisher procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding coercive self-citation and citation abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must not coerce authors into citing the reviewers’ own work as a condition for favorable review; such coercive self-citations and citation abuse are misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer genuinely believes a missing citation is essential, explain why and how it relates; declare any relationship to suggested citations. Editors should be alert to patterns of coercive self‑citation when assessing reviewer behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recognition and crediting mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms to motivate and credit reviewers include annual acknowledgments, certificates of excellence (CPD points), bonus points to discount open-access fees, and platforms like Publons (integrated with Web of Science) for recording validated reviewer accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may record contributions on Publons and link to ORCID. Journals and publishers can use acknowledgments, awards, or points systems to incentivize timely, high-quality reviews. Training resources (e.g., Publons Academy) are available for novice reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of editorial management systems in supporting review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial systems provide review instructions, structured forms, and access to bibliographic databases, enabling evidence-based comments that examine novelty, ethics, and implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the tools and structured forms provided to ensure completeness. Editors should configure systems to link reviewers to reporting checklists and resources to facilitate thorough assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of language proficiency in reviewer selection and comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are often requested to comment on language correctness and readability; however, language comments are generally categorized as minor, and poor language skills may exclude reviewers from top journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag major language issues that impede understanding but avoid focusing reviews on copy-editing. Non‑Anglophone reviewers should seek language training or mentorship to improve commenting skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of predatory publishing indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Unjustifiably short peer review timelines can indicate absence of quality evaluation and predatory publishing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consider a journal’s peer review strategy and timelines when selecting a target journal. Reviewers and editors should flag unusually rapid acceptance pipelines that bypass proper review.
